analysis.one_liner: Lifts campaign money limits and shields big donors' identities from disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referrals; with zero cosponsors, it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite campaign finance law to favor big money. It would erase the cap on political parties' coordinated spending, write the Supreme Court's McCutcheon decision into law so one donor could give to every party committee, lift various reporting thresholds, let internet political spending escape contribution and spending rules, and stop the Securities and Exchange Commission from ever requiring companies to disclose their political spending. It would also bar the federal government from collecting or releasing the names of donors to tax-exempt groups and stop the IRS from requiring most nonprofits to report contributors.
analysis.who_benefits: Large individual donors (who could give to every national and state party committee without a combined cap), the national and state party committees that would collect unlimited coordinated spending, corporations and trade associations (shielded from any SEC rule requiring disclosure of political contributions or dues), and 501(c) nonprofit groups that spend on politics without revealing their funders. Donors to tax-exempt groups would also gain a federal privacy guarantee backed by felony penalties for officials who leak their names.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy donors, party committees, and dark-money groups

how_it_helps.text: Repeals statutory limits on how much political party committees may spend in coordination with candidates, removing a ceiling on party spending in federal elections.

Repeals the aggregate limit on what one individual can contribute across all committees in a two-year cycle, giving statutory effect to McCutcheon v. FEC and letting a single donor max out to every party committee.

Raises state party contribution limits to match national party limits and expands the 'soft money'-style activity state and local parties may conduct, allowing money not subject to federal contribution limits to flow through state and local party committees unless it is coordinated with a federal candidate.

Prohibits the Securities and Exchange Commission from finalizing, issuing, or implementing any rule on disclosure of political contributions, contributions to tax-exempt organizations, or trade association dues, blocking the long-pending shareholder disclosure rulemaking.

Bars federal entities from collecting or publicly releasing the identities of donors to tax-exempt organizations, with criminal penalties of up to $250,000 in fines and five years in prison for willful disclosure.

Raises the gross-receipts threshold at which nonprofits must file IRS information returns from $5,000 to $50,000 and exempts most 501(c) organizations from reporting the names and addresses of contributors.
Exempts most unpaid internet communications from treatment as contributions or expenditures and expands the media exemption to internet-based publishers and platforms.

Raises the threshold at which a group becomes a regulated 'political committee' from $5,000 to $25,000, quadruples the independent-expenditure reporting threshold from $250 to $1,000, and repeals the requirement that independent spenders report identifying information about certain donors.
Sets a five-year statute of limitations on all proceedings to enforce the Federal Election Campaign Act, after which violations can no longer be penalized.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters, who would have less ability to see who is funding the campaigns and advocacy seeking to influence their votes. Limits that keep any single donor from dominating would be gone or raised, enforcement of existing campaign law would expire after five years, and shareholders would lose the chance to require companies to disclose political spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters who want to follow the money

drawbacks.text: Repealing the aggregate contribution cap and coordinated-spending limits would let a single wealthy donor fund every national and state party committee, concentrating influence over both parties' campaigns in very few hands.

The donor-privacy provisions would shield the funders of politically active tax-exempt groups, which may spend on elections and lobbying without disclosure, making it harder for voters to know who is behind campaign messages.

The five-year statute of limitations and raised reporting thresholds would weaken enforcement of the Federal Election Campaign Act, letting violations age out unprosecuted and keeping more spending off the books.
Blocking any SEC rule on political spending disclosure would leave shareholders without a federal mechanism to learn how companies spend their money on politics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does offer a genuine protection: federal officials could no longer compile or leak the names of donors to tax-exempt groups, which protects some small givers from harassment. But that benefit sits inside a package whose main effect is the opposite of transparency: uncapping coordinated party spending, letting one donor give to every committee, exempting internet spending from the definition of campaign spending, and cutting enforcement deadlines. For a voter trying to know who is trying to buy influence in their election, the net effect would be substantially worse.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and an elections subcommittee, and no committee ever reported it out or brought it to the floor before the term ended.

narrative.text: Representative Kelly Armstrong, a North Dakota Republican, introduced the bill on July 6, 2023, with the stated goal of protecting political speech on the theory that Congress may regulate political speech only to prevent corruption.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill, so it never had the backing of a second legislator.

The bill was referred to the House Administration, Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Oversight committees on the day of introduction, and in September 2023 it was referred to the Elections Subcommittee of House Administration.
No committee or subcommittee held a markup or vote, and the bill never received a floor vote in the House or Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary voters and disclosure advocates, because the existing contribution limits, coordinated-spending caps, and donor-reporting requirements stayed in place. Big donors, party committees, and politically active tax-exempt groups did not get the expanded channels the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure the split; support was limited to one Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so the bill's fate reflected inaction rather than a recorded party fight.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill would let party committees spend unlimited amounts in coordination with candidates and raise state party limits to national levels, channeling far more money through the parties. Voters would lose one of the main ceilings on how much money saturates their elections.

Repealing the aggregate two-year cap would let one wealthy donor legally max out to every party committee and candidate. The more concentrated campaign funding becomes, the less weight an ordinary voter's voice carries.

The bill would bar the government from collecting or disclosing donor identities, raise the IRS filing threshold to $50,000, and stop most nonprofits from reporting contributors, letting these groups raise and spend without anyone knowing who is behind them. It also freezes the 501(c)(4) social-welfare standard at its 2010 definition, preventing the Treasury from tightening it.

The bill would permanently block the Securities and Exchange Commission from issuing any rule on disclosure of corporate political contributions, tax-exempt contributions, or trade association dues. Shareholders and voters would have no federal route to see corporate political spending.

industries.industry: Internet platforms and digital political advertisers
industries.note: Unpaid internet communications would be exempt from being counted as contributions or expenditures, and the media exemption would extend to internet-based publishers and platforms. Political spending online could grow with less of it counted or disclosed under campaign law.
